result: Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer in women globally, resulting in 311,000 deaths in 2018, with the burden continuing to rise and falling disproportionately on women in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). The disease often affects young women who are primary wage earners, and many countries lack resources for treatment.
evaluation: Claims C1-C6 are all supported by appropriate citations to peer-reviewed literature and authoritative sources (Arbyn et al., 2020; Cohen et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2021; Union for International Cancer Control, 2023; American Society of Clinical Oncology, 2023; Reed et al., 2000). These claims establish the epidemiological context and burden of cervical cancer globally.

result: The WHO launched the Cervical Cancer Elimination Strategy in 2019 with the goal of reducing cervical cancer incidence from about 15 per 100,000 women to less than 4 per 100,000 by 2030. The strategy has three targets: 90% HPV vaccination coverage by age 15, 70% screening coverage with high-precision assays twice by age 45, and treating 90% of women with pre-cancer and managing 90% with invasive cancer.
evaluation: Claims C7-C11 accurately describe the WHO Cervical Cancer Elimination Strategy and its targets, supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2020. These are well-documented public health goals that form the foundation for the manuscript's discussion.

result: HPV vaccination will likely have the biggest impact on cervical cancer incidence in the long run, while screening and treatment will have bigger impacts in the short-term.
evaluation: Claims C12-C13 represent reasonable inferences based on the biological and temporal dynamics of HPV vaccination (preventing future infections) versus screening/treatment (detecting and treating existing disease). This is consistent with established public health understanding, though the claims are presented as inference rather than empirical data.

result: The COVID-19 pandemic severely disrupted cervical cancer prevention efforts globally, including vaccination programs, screening services, and treatment. Disruptions were caused by school closures, suspension of clinical services, fund redistribution, facility limitations, and patient fear of exposure. The impact was greater than some natural disasters, with LMICs experiencing the most severe and prolonged disruptions, and widespread healthcare worker burnout hindering recovery.
evaluation: Claims C14, C27-C35 are well-supported by multiple citations documenting pandemic impacts across different settings (Rao et al., 2022; Pillai, 2022; Daniels et al., 2021; Newton, 2021; Mayo et al., 2021; Carcopino et al., 2022; Dennis et al., 2021; Istrate-Ofiteru et al., 2021; Santos et al., 2021; Baaske et al., 2022; Schad et al., 2021; Ortiz et al., 2021; Basu et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2022; Miller et al., 2020; Amouzou et al., 2021; Murewanhema, 2021; Smith and Perkins, 2022). The evidence converges from multiple geographic regions and settings.

result: Cancer diagnoses were reduced during the pandemic, creating a backlog. A Romanian study reported more advanced cervical cancer presentations during the pandemic. Modeling studies from the UK and US predict increased cervical cancer burden regardless of catch-up time, with greater disparities expected in settings without capacity to augment services.
evaluation: Claims C36-C39 are supported by appropriate citations (Eskander et al., 2022; Popescu et al., 2022; Castanon et al., 2021b; Burger et al., 2021; Bonadio et al., 2021; Castanon et al., 2021a). The modeling studies provide evidence-based projections, though the actual long-term impact remains to be observed. The Romanian study provides empirical evidence of more advanced disease presentations.

result: Prior to the pandemic, only 60% of WHO member states had incorporated HPV vaccination into national schedules, with only 13% of girls completing vaccination. Coverage had not reached the 90% target in most countries due to health systems capacity challenges, and LMICs were disadvantaged by international supply chain limitations.
evaluation: Claims C15-C18 are supported by citations to WHO, 2022a; Amponsah-Dacosta et al., 2020; Garland et al., 2020; and Colzani et al., 2021. These claims establish the pre-pandemic baseline for HPV vaccination coverage and identify key barriers to achieving elimination strategy targets.

result: Prior to the pandemic, only 37% of countries achieved lifetime screening coverage of 70% or higher, with none being low-income countries. Coverage was proportional to country income strata: 58% of high-income countries, 28% of upper-middle-income, 6% of lower-middle-income, and 0% of low-income countries achieved 70% coverage. Only 75 of 202 surveyed countries achieved 70% coverage, with most African and South Asian countries having less than 20% coverage. Wide socioeconomic disparities exist within countries, particularly in opportunistic screening programs.
evaluation: Claims C19-C24 are supported by data from Bruni et al., 2022 and Figure 1, along with citations to Phaswana-Mafuya and Peltzer, 2018 and Corrêa et al., 2022. The data clearly demonstrate the stark disparities in screening coverage by country income level and geographic region, providing strong evidence for the inequitable distribution of cervical cancer prevention services.

result: Screening coverage is inversely correlated to cervical cancer incidence and mortality, with countries having the highest incidence (in sub-Saharan Africa, south Asia, and South America) largely corresponding to countries with low screening coverage.
evaluation: Claims C25-C26 are supported by citation to Arbyn et al., 2018 and Figure 2. The inverse correlation between screening coverage and cervical cancer burden is well-established in the literature and visually demonstrated in the provided figure. This represents a fundamental epidemiological relationship in cervical cancer prevention.

result: At the pandemic's start, screening in most countries required pelvic examination, which is difficult to make COVID-friendly due to 30-minute counseling/examination/treatment sessions in closed spaces, additional disinfection time between patients, and resulting reduced patient volume in clinics.
evaluation: Claims C40-C44 describe the practical challenges of cervical screening during the pandemic. While C40, C42, and C43 are stated as general knowledge, C44 is supported by citation to Sormani et al., 2021. The inference in C41 about difficulty making pelvic exams COVID-friendly is reasonable given the described constraints. These claims logically explain why cervical screening was particularly vulnerable during the pandemic.

result: Pre-pandemic screening modalities varied by country income level: cytology was most prevalent in high-income countries (78%), while VIA was most common in LMICs. Only 35% of country strategies planned to include HPV testing, and just 17 countries had introduced HPV self-sampling by October 2020, with half restricting it to under-screened populations. HPV self-sampling and primary screening were mostly concentrated in high-income countries.
evaluation: Claims C45-C51 are supported by citations to Bruni et al., 2022 and Serrano et al., 2022, with visual evidence from Figure 3. The data clearly demonstrate disparities in screening technology adoption, with more advanced HPV-based approaches concentrated in high-income countries. This establishes the pre-pandemic baseline for screening technology distribution.

result: A new model for cervical cancer prevention services was needed before the pandemic, but this need has been magnified by the post-pandemic backlog. Population-level HPV self-testing is the most cost-effective long-term approach, though upfront affordability and cost-effective triage strategies remain challenges. Programs focused on short-term costs and outcomes likely miss the mark on effective programming.
evaluation: Claims C52-C55 are supported by citation to Mezei et al., 2017 regarding cost-effectiveness of HPV self-testing. Claims C52, C53, and C56 are presented as inferences about the need for new approaches and limitations of short-term thinking. While these are opinion-based claims, they are reasonable given the documented challenges in achieving elimination strategy targets and the pandemic's impact.

result: COVID-19 exposed existing inequities in global health resource access but also provided a model for coordinated funding and policy development. While many countries initially failed to get adequate vaccine due to high-income country dominance of early supply, the acute need drove increased manufacturing efficiency, and global coordination led to interventions including trade agreements, equipment procurement, and manufacturing scale-up in countries without prior capacity.
evaluation: Claims C57-C61 are supported by citations to McGowan and Bambra, 2022; Pasquale et al., 2021; Stolberg, 2022; Foundation for Innovative New Diagnostics, 2023; World Health Organization, 2022b; Tatar et al., 2021; and World Health Organization, 2022c. These claims accurately describe both the failures and successes of the COVID-19 response, providing context for lessons applicable to cervical cancer elimination.

result: The pandemic drove innovations in diagnostic access including supply chain diversification, emergency use listing, price negotiations, and rapid implementation of testing protocols available without provider visits. Screening outside health facilities became routine, including self-testing at home and in community settings. There was increased individual health self-efficacy, direct patient result reporting, population acceptance of self-testing through public health messaging, increased telehealth utilization, community health worker engagement, and private sector involvement in public health programming.
evaluation: Claims C62-C71 describe pandemic-era innovations and behavioral changes. Several are supported by citations (C63: The Global Fund, 2022; C65: Feletto et al., 2020; C69: Covid-19 Information Center, 2022), while others (C62, C64, C66, C68, C70, C71) are stated as general knowledge about pandemic responses. Claim C67 about increased self-efficacy is presented as inference. These claims collectively describe well-documented shifts in healthcare delivery and patient engagement during the pandemic.

result: The pandemic drove efforts to reduce LMIC dependence on global production by increasing local testing capacity. This resulted in initiatives to start and scale up rapid diagnostic production in Latin America, Africa, and Asia at more affordable prices. Twenty African countries could sequence SARS-CoV-2 by April 2020, with Botswana and South Africa first detecting the Omicron variant. Investment in laboratory and bioinformatic personnel training contributed to lasting, translatable capacity.
evaluation: Claims C72-C76 are supported by citations to UNITAID, 2021; Viana et al., 2022; and Tegally et al., 2022. These claims document important capacity-building achievements during the pandemic, particularly in LMICs, which are relevant to potential applications for cervical cancer prevention. The evidence demonstrates concrete examples of technology transfer and capacity development.

result: HPV vaccination programs will require catch-up periods with expanded age cohorts to reach children who missed vaccination. COVID-19 vaccination infrastructure may facilitate HPV vaccination through established supply chains and community-based teams. Innovation in COVID-19 vaccines may create momentum for HPV vaccine supply. Increased supply, logistical capacity, and single-dose HPV schedule data may facilitate school- and community-based vaccination for eligible children and catch-up populations.
evaluation: Claim C77 is a reasonable inference about needed catch-up vaccination. However, claims C78-C80 are largely speculative (marked as SPECULATION in evidence_type), using conditional language like "may facilitate" and "may have created momentum." While C80 cites supporting evidence (The Lancet Oncology, 2022; Toh et al., 2021) for single-dose schedules, the overall claims about leveraging COVID-19 infrastructure for HPV vaccination remain hypothetical and unproven. These are recommendations rather than demonstrated results.

result: Multiple HPV assays exist for self-sampling but await clinical validation. COVID-19-driven increases in molecular testing production, platforms, laboratory capacity, and manufacturing could contribute to increased HPV testing capacity. Point-of-care molecular diagnostic innovation may facilitate accessible test-and-treat services. Manufacturing diagnostics and vaccines in LMICs could expand accessibility. Demonstration projects have shown success with community-based screening and mail-in HPV self-collection.
evaluation: Claim C81 is supported by citation to Wentzensen et al., 2021 regarding existing but unvalidated assays. Claims C82-C84 are largely speculative ("could contribute," "may facilitate," "has the potential"), though supported by citations (Poljak et al., 2021; Foundation for Innovative New Diagnostics, 2021). Claim C85 is supported by multiple citations documenting successful demonstration projects (Woo et al., 2022; Castle et al., 2011; Ejegod et al., 2022; Winer et al., 2019; Ngu et al., 2022). However, the overall result conflates demonstrated successes in limited settings with speculative potential for broader application.

result: Moving to high-performance HPV testing will require coordinated work in R&D, product development, IP management, pre-qualification, manufacturing, and regulatory approval. Targeted investment in point-of-care HPV testing and regulatory approval of self-sampling are needed to enable test-and-treat programs. Point-of-care HPV diagnostics would ideally replace VIA programs and enable high-performance testing in countries without existing programs. Test-and-treat programs offering same-day treatment would be more efficient by narrowing the pool needing triage. Coordinated innovation needs price negotiations to ensure affordable, equitable distribution.
evaluation: Claims C86-C87 are supported by citations to World Health Organization, 2022c; Lim, 2021; and World Health Organization, 2022d. Claims C88-C90 are presented as inferences about optimal strategies. While these are recommendations rather than demonstrated results, they are logical extensions of established principles in cervical cancer screening and represent reasonable policy positions based on the evidence presented about current screening disparities and technology availability.

result: Coordinated research on HPV triage using pooled genotyping, biomarkers, methylation, and AI is necessary for effective programming. Country-level cost analysis using open-access tools will be necessary to ensure integration of effective technologies. Patient navigation to ensure HPV-positive women return for triage and treatment is essential. Risk-based approaches to triage and diagnosis may increase efficiency and implementation of effective screening programs.
evaluation: Claims C91, C93, and C94 are presented as inferences about necessary program components, with C94 supported by citation to Ribeiro et al., 2021. Claim C92 is supported by citation to Herrick et al., 2022 regarding cost analysis tools. While these are recommendations rather than demonstrated results, they represent reasonable evidence-based policy positions. The claims identify key components needed for successful HPV-based screening programs.

result: Information, education, and communication needs to be innovative and tailored to how different groups obtain information. Information must be understandable without complex explanations and delivered outside healthcare settings through community health workers, word-of-mouth, peer counseling, and online platforms. Working with traditional leaders and established societal structures is critical for disseminating information and engendering trust.
evaluation: Claim C96 is supported by citations to Eala and Tantengco, 2022; Ciceron et al., 2022; De Bocanegra et al., 2022; and Christie-de Jong et al., 2022. Claims C95 and C97 are presented as inferences about communication requirements. These recommendations are consistent with established principles of health communication and community engagement, particularly for reaching underserved populations.

result: COVID-19 forced rapid development of web-based systems adaptable to cervical screening programs. Brazil demonstrated success with automated call-and-recall systems for screening invitations, results, and appointments. Bangladesh monitored cervical screening using customized DHIS2 platform. Technological innovation can optimize population-level HPV self-sampling implementation and facilitate program monitoring and evaluation.
evaluation: Claims C98-C100 are supported by citations to Dixon et al., 2022; Corrêa et al., 2022; and Basu et al., 2021, providing concrete examples of technological innovations applied to cervical screening. Claim C101 is partially speculative ("can optimize") but supported by citation to Woo et al., 2021. The examples from Brazil and Bangladesh demonstrate proof-of-concept for technology-enabled screening programs, though broader implementation remains to be demonstrated.

result: Cervical cancer elimination success requires strong health systems with long-term strategies beyond innovation and technology. The COVID-19 response failed in health systems integration, gathering international organizations without global representation or sufficient perspective on variable health systems. Top-down global policy not contextualized in national planning is ineffective long-term and perpetuates disparities. Without meaningful country involvement and national planning rooted in dynamic health systems, elimination will fail. Prioritizing national autonomy in designing programming aligned with national goals, then leveraging global resources, is more likely to succeed. Global coordination will only succeed if countries most impacted are at the table.
evaluation: Claims C103-C104 are supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2022b regarding failures of COVID-19 response. Claims C102, C105-C108 are presented as inferences about requirements for successful elimination efforts. While these are opinion-based policy positions, they are reasonable conclusions drawn from documented failures in COVID-19 response and persistent disparities in cervical cancer prevention. The emphasis on country ownership and meaningful participation reflects established principles of effective global health programming.

result: The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated that controlling an infectious disease is possible when local, national, and global entities respond to people's needs. The successes provided momentum and the failures forced re-evaluation of meaningful engagement.
evaluation: Claims C109-C110 are presented as inferences from the pandemic experience. While these are interpretive statements rather than empirical findings, they represent reasonable conclusions supported by the extensive evidence presented throughout the manuscript about both successes (vaccine development, diagnostic innovation, capacity building) and failures (inequitable access, lack of country representation) of the COVID-19 response. These claims synthesize lessons learned for application to cervical cancer elimination.
